title: Google AI Plus Student Plan 2026: Free 1-Year AI Access for Tertiary Students in Ghana and 26 Other African Countries
summary: Google has brought back its Google AI Plus student offer, giving eligible tertiary students across 27 Sub-Saharan African countries the opportunity to access Google AI Plus at no cost for one year. The offer is designed to help students study, conduct research, organise their coursework, prepare for examinations, improve their writing, and use advanced AI tools for academic and creative projects. For students who regularly work with lecture notes, textbooks, presentations, research papers, assignments, and other academic materials, the offer provides access to a collection of AI-powered learning tools within Google s ecosystem. Eligible students can benefit from higher usage limits, unlimited uploads of study materials, 400 GB of cloud storage, interactive visualisations, personalised study notebooks, Gemini Live, Deep Research, image generation, video generation, and other AI-powered features during the promotional period. Google AI Plus Student Offer The Google AI Plus student plan gives eligible students access to enhanced Gemini capabilities and additional Google services for one year at no cost. The offer is particularly relevant to tertiary students who want to incorporate AI into their academic workflow, whether they need help understanding difficult concepts, preparing for an examination, analysing course materials, conducting research, or improving written work. Rather than simply providing a general-purpose chatbot, Google s student-focused tools allow students to upload their own learning materials and use them as the basis for personalised study activities. What Does the Google AI Plus Student Plan Include? Eligible students can access several features intended to support different aspects of student life and academic work. 1. Higher Usage Limits The student offer provides higher usage limits, allowing eligible students to make greater use of Google s AI tools for studying, research, writing, and other tasks. This can be particularly useful for students who need to work with AI regularly throughout a semester rather than only occasionally. 2. Unlimited Uploads of Study Materials One of the key features highlighted in the student offer is the ability to upload course materials. Students can upload materials such as: Lecture notes Course documents Study guides Presentations Research materials Images Other relevant academic files Once materials have been uploaded, students can use Gemini to analyse and work with the content. For example, a student preparing for an examination could upload lecture notes and ask Gemini to create a study guide, generate practice questions, explain difficult topics, or quiz them on the material. Personalised Study Notebooks Students can create study notebooks for individual courses and organise their learning materials in one place. Gemini can use uploaded course materials to help create a learning plan tailored to the student s content and study needs. This can make it easier for students to move from simply collecting notes to actively studying and testing their understanding. Personalised Quizzes Students can turn their notes and other course materials into personalised quizzes. Instead of manually creating practice questions, students can ask Gemini to generate questions based on the materials they have uploaded. This can be useful when preparing for examinations because students can test themselves on the specific content covered in their courses. Performance Tracking The student tools can also help students identify areas where they may need additional study. By using personalised quizzes and study activities, students can identify topics they understand well and areas that require further revision. Interactive Visualisations for Learning Another feature of the Google AI Plus student experience is interactive visualisation. Some academic concepts can be difficult to understand through written explanations alone. Interactive visualisations can provide another way of exploring how concepts work. For example, students may be able to use visual explanations when studying scientific, mathematical, technical, or other complex subjects. This approach can make abstract ideas easier to explore and understand by allowing students to see concepts represented visually. Gemini Live for Real-Time Learning The offer also provides access to Gemini Live , which allows students to have real-time conversations with Gemini. Students can use conversational interaction to ask questions about difficult concepts and receive explanations as they study. For example, a student who does not understand a particular topic can ask Gemini to explain it in simpler language, provide examples, or approach the concept from a different perspective. This can make AI assistance feel more like an interactive study session rather than simply receiving a written response. AI-Powered Homework Help Google s student tools can also be used to support homework and assignments. Students can upload an image or file of the work they are doing and ask Gemini for assistance. Examples of possible prompts include: Walk me through the solution for this maths problem. Explain this concept step by step. Help me understand this diagram. Explain the historical significance of this painting. Explain how DNA replication works. The goal is not simply to provide an answer but to help students understand how to arrive at a solution. Exam Preparation Preparing for examinations is another major use case for the student plan. Students can upload their course materials and use Gemini to create different types of revision resources. These can include: Study guides Practice tests Personalised quizzes Topic summaries Question-and-answer exercises Audio overviews Explanations of difficult concepts For example, a student could upload lecture notes and ask Gemini to create a practice examination based entirely on those notes. Students can also ask Gemini to quiz them on a particular subject or topic, allowing them to practise recalling information before an examination. Deep Research for Academic Work The offer also provides access to Deep Research , which can assist students with more extensive research tasks. Students may use research-oriented AI tools to explore academic topics, investigate historical developments, gather information, and develop a better understanding of complex subjects. For example, students could request research into a historical event, scientific topic, social issue, or other academic subject. Students should still evaluate AI-generated information carefully and verify important facts using reliable academic and primary sources. Writing and Academic Support Google AI Plus can also assist students with writing-related tasks. Students can use Gemini throughout different stages of the writing process, from brainstorming ideas to polishing a final draft. Possible uses include: Brainstorming ideas for assignments Developing an essay outline Proofreading written work Suggesting improvements to an essay Improving clarity and structure Making an email more professional Polishing a CV Developing content for student organisations Creating ideas for websites and digital projects This makes the tools useful beyond conventional studying and can also support students with career preparation and professional communication. Image and Video Generation The student offer also highlights access to AI-powered image and video generation tools. These capabilities can be useful for students working on presentations, creative projects, educational materials, visual explanations, and other forms of digital content. Students studying subjects that benefit from visual learning can potentially use generated images and visual content to explore ideas in new ways. 400 GB Cloud Storage Eligible students can also receive 400 GB of cloud storage as part of the offer. The additional storage can be useful for students who need to keep large numbers of academic documents, presentations, images, research materials, and other digital files. Having additional cloud storage can also help students keep important files accessible across their devices. Connected Google Apps The Google AI ecosystem can connect with services such as Gmail, Drive, and Google Workspace. For students already using Google s productivity tools for academic work, these integrations can help connect information across different services. This can be particularly useful for students who use Google Drive to store course materials or Gmail to communicate with lecturers, classmates, departments, and organisations. Examples of How Students Can Use Google AI Plus There are many ways students can incorporate the tools into their academic routines. For studying Upload lecture notes and ask Gemini to: Summarise key concepts Explain difficult sections Generate revision questions Create a study guide Identify important topics For examination preparation Students can: Create practice tests Generate personalised quizzes Ask Gemini to quiz them interactively Identify weak areas Review difficult concepts For research Students can: Explore unfamiliar topics Conduct deeper research Organise research information Ask questions about uploaded documents Develop research ideas For assignments Students can: Brainstorm ideas Create outlines Improve writing Proofread drafts Clarify complex concepts Review their work before submission For career preparation Students can also use the tools to: Polish their CV Improve professional emails Brainstorm career ideas Prepare written materials Develop digital projects Who Can Apply for the Google AI Plus Student Offer? The offer is intended for eligible tertiary students aged 18 and above in participating Sub-Saharan African countries. The promotion states that students across 27 Sub-Saharan African countries are eligible, subject to Google s eligibility requirements and offer terms. This means the opportunity is targeted at students in higher education rather than the general public. Students should confirm their eligibility during the registration process because additional requirements may apply. title: OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship 2026 in Warsaw: Applications Open for a Six-Month Placement
summary: The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe is accepting applications for its 2026 Human Rights Internship at the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights in Warsaw, Poland. This full-time, six-month placement is expected to begin in November 2026 and will give a graduate-level student or recent graduate the opportunity to support ODIHR’s Human Rights Department. The placement is particularly relevant to emerging professionals interested in international human rights, political science, law, international relations, human rights monitoring, democratic governance and related disciplines. Interns will support research, analysis, written reporting, event organization and the implementation of human rights programmes across the OSCE region. According to the official OSCE vacancy announcement , applications must be submitted by 3 September 2026 . Candidates must also state their availability dates in their cover letter. OSCE ODIHR Internship 2026 at a Glance Official position title: Intern Issuing office: Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Department: Human Rights Department Duty station: Warsaw, Poland Requisition number: ODI000321 Job field: Human Rights Schedule: Full-time Employment status: Short-term Grade: No grade Internship duration: Six months Expected starting period: November 2026 Issue date: 20 August 2026 Application deadline: 3 September 2026 Number of posts: The vacancy metadata lists two posts, although the main description says that the department is seeking one intern. Applicants should consult the official vacancy page for any clarification or subsequent correction. Application method: Online through the OSCE recruitment portal About the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights The Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, commonly known as ODIHR, is one of the principal institutions of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe. ODIHR is responsible for supporting the human dimension of the OSCE’s comprehensive approach to security. The human dimension recognizes that lasting peace and security depend not only on political and military stability, but also on democracy, respect for human rights, the rule of law and strong public institutions. ODIHR provides assistance, expertise and practical support to governments, public institutions and civil society organizations. Its activities include: Observing elections and assessing electoral processes; Supporting the development of democratic institutions; Reviewing legislation and advising governments; Promoting the rule of law; Monitoring and strengthening respect for human rights; Supporting tolerance and non-discrimination; Conducting training for government officials, law-enforcement personnel and civil society representatives; and Helping participating States implement their OSCE human dimension commitments. ODIHR’s activities are implemented across the OSCE’s 57 participating States. More information about its institutional mandate is available through ODIHR’s official human-dimension overview . About the ODIHR Human Rights Department The successful intern will be placed in ODIHR’s Human Rights Department. The department provides expert advice to OSCE participating States, organizes capacity-building initiatives and monitors the implementation of human dimension commitments. Its work involves engagement with State authorities, national institutions, civil society representatives, human rights defenders, researchers and other stakeholders. The department’s programmes cover a broad range of thematic human rights priorities, including: Human rights defenders ODIHR works to strengthen the ability of human rights defenders to conduct their legitimate activities safely and effectively. This includes monitoring the challenges defenders face and supporting participating States in fulfilling their responsibilities to protect them. Human rights education Activities in this area seek to improve awareness, understanding and practical application of human rights standards among public officials, law-enforcement personnel, educators, civil society organizations and other groups. Human rights and counter-terrorism ODIHR promotes approaches to preventing and countering terrorism that comply with international human rights standards and OSCE commitments. Torture prevention The department contributes to work intended to prevent torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. This may involve research, monitoring, institutional support and capacity-building. Anti-trafficking work ODIHR addresses the human rights dimensions of trafficking in human beings, including the protection of victims, access to justice and the development of rights-based responses. Freedom of religion or belief Programmes in this area support the right of individuals and communities to adopt, practise, change or manifest their religion or belief without discrimination or unjustified interference. Freedom of peaceful assembly ODIHR monitors developments and supports participating States in protecting the right to organize and participate in peaceful assemblies. National human rights institutions The department supports institutions mandated to promote and protect human rights at the national level, including through capacity development and the promotion of institutional independence. Human rights, gender and security This area considers the relationship between human rights, gender equality and security policies, including the need to incorporate gender perspectives into institutional and programme activities. The selected intern may contribute to one or several of these programmes depending on departmental priorities and operational needs. Main Responsibilities of the Human Rights Intern The intern will assist with the implementation of activities conducted by the Human Rights Department. The responsibilities combine research, writing, project support and administrative coordination. 1. Conducting desk research and human rights analysis The intern will research human rights developments relevant to OSCE participating States. This research will assist ODIHR in monitoring how States implement their OSCE human dimension commitments. The work may require the intern to: Identify relevant information from credible public sources; Review laws, policies, reports and institutional developments; Follow country-specific and regional human rights developments; Organize research findings in a clear and accessible format; Distinguish between verified information and unconfirmed claims; and Support the preparation of internal or public-facing analysis. The vacancy therefore requires someone who can work carefully with complex information, recognize relevant developments and communicate findings accurately. 2. Assisting with reports, briefing papers and other documents The intern will help prepare reports, briefing materials and other written products dealing with thematic, national or regional human rights issues. Assignments may include: Collecting and organizing background information; Summarizing longer reports and source materials; Preparing initial drafts or sections of documents; Editing and formatting written materials; Checking facts, references and consistency; Supporting the development of country or regional briefings; and Contributing to documents on specific human rights themes. Strong analytical writing is therefore central to the placement. Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate that they can convert research findings into structured, concise and evidence-based written material. 3. Supporting meetings, conferences, workshops and events The intern will assist with the preparation and organization of activities managed by the Human Rights Department. This may involve support before, during and after events, including: Conducting background research; Helping prepare agendas and supporting materials; Organizing documents for participants; Assisting with logistical or administrative preparations; Supporting communication with relevant colleagues and stakeholders; Helping ensure that event materials are properly organized; and Contributing to follow-up documentation. The role consequently requires attention to detail, reliability, communication skills and the ability to manage multiple tasks within established deadlines. 4. Taking notes and contributing to event reports During meetings, conferences, workshops and other activities, the intern may be asked to take accurate notes and help prepare written records. Effective note-taking in this context means identifying: The central issues discussed; Significant observations made by participants; Recommendations or proposed actions; Areas of agreement or disagreement; Follow-up responsibilities; and Information that should be reflected in an event report. Applicants with previous experience preparing meeting minutes, workshop reports, academic summaries or conference documentation may be especially well positioned for this responsibility. 5. Supporting additional programme and department-wide activities The intern may also support other projects, tasks and department-wide activities as assigned. This provision reflects the varied nature of work in an international organization. The selected candidate should therefore be flexible, able to respond to changing priorities and willing to assist across different human rights themes when necessary. Educational Requirements Applicants must fall within one of the academic categories specified in the vacancy notice. Eligible candidates include: Students in the final year of higher education at the graduate or postgraduate level in a university or another accredited institution; or Recent graduates or postgraduates who completed their studies within the previous two years. Relevant fields of study include: Political science; International relations; Law; International human rights law; or Another closely related discipline. A qualification in a different field may still be relevant if the applicant can demonstrate a clear connection between their studies and ODIHR’s human rights mandate. Candidates should explain that connection directly in their application rather than expecting recruiters to infer it. Age and Nationality Requirements Applicants must meet the following mandatory conditions: They must not be older than 30 years. They must be nationals of an OSCE participating State. Nationality is the controlling requirement. Living, studying or working in an OSCE participating State does not necessarily make someone eligible if they are not a national of one of the participating States. The complete and current list is available on the official OSCE participating States page . Required Skills and Competencies In addition to meeting the academic, age and nationality conditions, applicants should demonstrate the following qualifications. Excellent English-language proficiency An excellent command of spoken and written English is required. The intern will undertake research, prepare written material, communicate with colleagues and contribute to reports in an international professional environment. Applicants should be able to: Read and understand complex human rights material; Write clearly and accurately; Summarize detailed information; Communicate professionally; and use appropriate terminology consistently. Russian-language knowledge Knowledge of Russian is considered an asset rather than a mandatory requirement. Candidates without Russian-language ability are not automatically excluded if they meet the essential requirements. Applicants who speak Russian should clearly state their proficiency level and indicate whether they can use the language for research, reading, writing or professional communication. Research and analytical writing ability Candidates must demonstrate competence in research and analytical writing. Relevant evidence could include: Academic research papers; A thesis or dissertation; Policy briefs; Legal research; Human rights reports; Country or regional analysis; Research assistance; Monitoring reports; or Publications produced through employment, volunteering or civil society work. Organizational, communication and reporting skills The successful candidate must be capable of organizing information and supporting activities in a structured manner. Applicants should provide examples showing that they can: Work according to deadlines; Prioritize assignments; Communicate with different audiences; Prepare accurate written reports; Maintain organized records; and Contribute to meetings, workshops or projects. Cultural sensitivity and sound judgment Because ODIHR works across a diverse regional and institutional environment, the intern must demonstrate cultural sensitivity and good judgment. This includes respecting different experiences and perspectives, communicating professionally and handling sensitive human rights information responsibly. Understanding of gender mainstreaming Applicants should understand the importance of integrating gender perspectives into policies, programmes, analysis and organizational activities. This does not necessarily require a specialized gender-studies degree, but candidates should be able to demonstrate awareness of how laws, policies and security or human rights developments can affect people differently. Computer proficiency Applicants must be able to use Windows-based applications, including: Word-processing software; Microsoft Excel; Email applications; and Other basic office productivity tools. The role may involve drafting and formatting reports, organizing information, maintaining records and communicating electronically with colleagues and stakeholders. Is Previous Human Rights Experience Mandatory? Previous exposure to or experience in human rights issues is identified as an asset, not as an absolute requirement. Potentially relevant experience could come from: A university research project; A human rights course or academic specialization; An internship with a civil society organization; Volunteer work; A legal clinic; Student leadership; Election observation; Work with a national human rights institution; Participation in advocacy or awareness campaigns; Research on democracy, governance, equality or fundamental freedoms; or Professional work involving related policy or legal questions. Applicants with limited formal work experience should not automatically assume they are unqualified. Academic research, volunteering and extracurricular activities can help demonstrate a serious engagement with human rights issues. Professional Development Value of the Placement The OSCE Internship Programme is designed to expose graduate-level students and recent graduates to the Organization’s work while allowing its institutions and departments to benefit from specialized assistance. Through this placement, the selected intern can gain practical exposure to: International human rights monitoring; Research on the implementation of political commitments; The preparation of reports and briefing papers; Country-specific and thematic analysis; International meeting and event organization; Professional note-taking and reporting; Multicultural teamwork; and The operations of an international security and human rights institution. The OSCE’s official internship information explains that its internship programme is intended to help graduate and postgraduate students or recent graduates develop professional skills and obtain practical experience in an international environment. However, applicants should understand that the internship does not create a commitment or guarantee of future employment with the OSCE. Duration, Schedule and Expected Starting Date The internship will last for six months and is expected to begin in November 2026. The position is full-time and based at ODIHR in Warsaw, Poland. The vacancy does not describe the placement as remote or hybrid, so applicants should prepare on the basis that they will need to be available at the duty station. The announced starting date is subject to change. Applicants must state their availability dates in their cover letter. This should be done clearly and specifically. For example, candidates can indicate: Their earliest possible starting date; Whether they are available from November 2026; Whether they can remain for the full six-month period; and Any academic or administrative obligations that could affect their availability. Remuneration and Living-Cost Support Applicants should review the financial terms carefully before applying. The OSCE states that it is not in a position to: Pay remuneration to the intern; Cover expenses incurred during the internship; Pay relocation costs; or Reimburse travel expenses. The placement should therefore not be treated as a salaried position. Nevertheless, interns who do not reside at the duty station may receive some compensation toward their cost of living. The stated amount is equivalent to 10 per cent of the applicable Daily Subsistence Allowance rate for Warsaw. This contribution should not be interpreted as a salary or as full financial support. Applicants should assess whether they can cover accommodation, food, local transportation, visa-related expenses where applicable, travel to Warsaw and other personal costs. The notice does not promise accommodation, relocation support or full living-cost coverage. Health, Life and Accident Insurance The selected intern may participate in the OSCE group health insurance scheme at their own expense. Alternatively, an intern who arranges independent medical insurance must provide evidence that the coverage is valid for: The Warsaw duty station; and Any destinations connected with possible official duty travel. The OSCE will cover life insurance and accident or disability insurance for the intern. Candidates should examine the scope, exclusions and duration of any personal medical policy before the placement begins. Insurance should remain valid throughout the internship period. How to Apply for the OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship Applications must be submitted through the OSCE’s online recruitment platform. Interested candidates should access the official vacancy page and select the application option provided there. A practical application process is as follows: Review the complete vacancy notice Confirm that you meet the academic status, age, nationality, language and skills requirements before beginning the application. Create or update your OSCE applicant profile Enter accurate personal, academic and professional information. Ensure that dates, qualification titles and institutional names are consistent throughout the application. Tailor your application to the Human Rights Department Explain how your studies, research, employment, volunteering or extracurricular activities relate to ODIHR’s human rights programmes. Demonstrate the required skills with examples Instead of merely stating that you have research, writing or organizational skills, describe a project or assignment through which you used them. Prepare a focused cover letter The cover letter should explain your motivation, relevant background and potential contribution to ODIHR. Most importantly, it must state your availability dates. Check your language and supporting information Proofread the application carefully. Human rights research and reporting require accuracy, so errors in the application could weaken the evidence of your written communication skills. Submit before the deadline Complete the online submission by 3 September 2026. The notice does not specify an exact closing time or time zone, so candidates should avoid waiting until the final hours. How to Strengthen Your Application The following measures are not additional eligibility requirements, but they can help applicants present their experience more effectively. Connect your background to specific ODIHR themes Rather than discussing human rights only in general terms, identify the areas most closely connected to your studies or experience, such as: Human rights defenders; Freedom of peaceful assembly; Freedom of religion or belief; Gender and security; Torture prevention; Anti-trafficking; Human rights education; National human rights institutions; or Human rights-compliant counter-terrorism. Provide evidence of analytical writing Mention specific written work you have completed, such as a dissertation, research paper, legal memorandum, policy brief or monitoring report. Explain the subject, research method and final output. Show that you can support events and teamwork If you have helped organize a seminar, student conference, workshop, advocacy event or public discussion, describe your responsibilities and the result. Address the financial conditions realistically Because the placement is not salaried and the possible living-cost contribution is limited, applicants should make an informed plan for spending six months in Warsaw. State your availability precisely Do not use vague wording. Clearly confirm whether you can begin in November 2026 and remain for the full placement. Selection Process and Communication Only candidates selected to participate in subsequent stages of recruitment will be contacted. Submitting an application does not guarantee an interview or further communication. Applicants should ensure that the email address and telephone details provided in their profile remain active. The OSCE also retains the discretion to: Re-advertise or repost the vacancy; Cancel the recruitment process; Offer an internship with modified terms of reference; or Change the duration of the internship. Applicants should monitor their email and the official recruitment portal for updates. Important Clarification About the Number of Positions The official listing contains an apparent inconsistency concerning the number of available places. The main description says that the Human Rights Department is seeking to recruit one intern. However, the “Additional Information” section lists the number of posts as two. Applicants should not rely on an unofficial interpretation of this difference. The vacancy remains a valid opportunity regardless of whether one or two candidates are ultimately appointed, and any updated information published by the OSCE should take precedence. Diversity, Inclusion and Professional Conduct The OSCE states that it is committed to diversity and inclusion within its workforce. Qualified female and male candidates from different religious, ethnic and social backgrounds are encouraged to apply. Candidates selected by the Organization are expected to conduct themselves in a manner appropriate to the status of international civil servants. This includes avoiding conduct that could undermine the integrity, independence or impartiality of their official functions. The OSCE Competency Model identifies commitment, diversity, integrity and accountability as core organizational values. It also emphasizes communication, collaboration, planning, analysis, sound decision-making, initiative and flexibility. Application Fee and Fraud Warning The OSCE does not request payment at any point in the application or review process. Candidates should submit their information only through the official OSCE recruitment system and should be cautious of individuals, websites or messages requesting money in exchange for application processing, interviews or guaranteed selection. Application Deadline The application deadline for the OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship is: 3 September 2026 Because the official announcement does not provide an exact closing time or time zone, applicants should submit well before the deadline. Applications should be made through the official OSCE internship vacancy page . Final Application Checklist Before submitting, confirm that: You are in the final year of graduate or postgraduate study, or graduated within the previous two years; Your academic field is political science, international relations, law, international human rights law or another related discipline; You are not older than 30; You are a national of an OSCE participating State; You have an excellent command of written and spoken English; You have described any Russian-language ability accurately; You have provided evidence of research and analytical writing skills; You have demonstrated organizational, communication and reporting abilities; You have addressed cultural sensitivity and gender mainstreaming where relevant; You can use standard Windows and Microsoft Office applications; Your cover letter states your exact availability; You have considered the financial and insurance conditions; Your contact information is accurate; and You have submitted the application by 3 September 2026. Conclusion The OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship 2026 offers graduate-level students and recent graduates an opportunity to contribute to research, reporting, events and programme implementation within one of Europe’s leading human rights and democratic institutions. The placement is especially suitable for candidates seeking practical exposure to international human rights monitoring, analytical writing, democratic governance and the implementation of OSCE human dimension commitments. It can also provide valuable experience working in a multicultural institutional environment and engaging with complex country-specific and thematic human rights questions. Candidates should nevertheless consider the terms carefully. The internship is full-time, based in Warsaw and not salaried. Travel and other personal expenses will not be reimbursed, while the possible living-cost contribution is limited to qualifying non-resident interns. Eligible candidates who can commit to the full six-month period should prepare a tailored application, state their availability clearly and submit through the official OSCE portal no later than 3 September 2026 . title: Green Growth Africa Recruitment 2026: Applications Open for Three Climate and Sustainable Development Jobs in Ghana
summary: Green Growth Africa has announced a new recruitment drive for three professional positions supporting its environmental, social, economic and community-development work in Ghana. The organisation is recruiting a Circularity and Just Transition Officer, an Integrated Development Officer, and a Research and Policy Officer. These positions offer qualified professionals an opportunity to contribute to climate resilience, circular economy development, environmental policy, community empowerment, evidence generation, local livelihoods and inclusive development. The deadline for applications is 28 August 2026. Green Growth Africa has stated that preference will be given to applicants currently based in Cape Coast or candidates prepared to relocate. The positions have not been advertised as remote opportunities, so applicants should be ready to work physically in Ghana. The detailed terms of reference supplied for the Integrated Development Officer and Research and Policy Officer confirm that both are full-time, one-year positions scheduled to begin on 1 October 2026. They may be renewed depending on satisfactory performance. Green Growth Africa Recruitment 2026 at a Glance Recruitment detail Confirmed information Recruiting organisation Green Growth Africa Number of advertised positions Three Country of employment Ghana Location preference Applicants from Cape Coast or candidates willing to relocate Application deadline 28 August 2026 Application closing time Not stated Application method Online application form Confirmed employment type Full-time for the Integrated Development and Research and Policy roles Confirmed start date 1 October 2026 for the Integrated Development and Research and Policy roles Confirmed initial contract One year for the two roles with available terms of reference Possible renewal Yes, subject to satisfactory performance Confirmed monthly compensation GHS 4,500–5,000 for the Integrated Development and Research and Policy roles Application documents CV and cover letter merged into one application document Recruitment contact info@greengrowthafrica.org Telephone enquiries +233 27 392 5309 The salary, start date, contract duration and detailed academic requirements for the Circularity and Just Transition Officer were not included in the documents supplied for review. Positions Available Green Growth Africa is accepting applications for the following positions: Circularity and Just Transition Officer Integrated Development Officer Research and Policy Officer The three positions address different but closely connected aspects of Green Growth Africa’s environmental and development mandate. The official recruitment announcement confirms that all three roles are part of the same application cycle and share an application deadline of 28 August 2026. About Green Growth Africa Green Growth Africa is a nonprofit and non-governmental organisation working to advance socioeconomic, environmental and technological development in underserved rural and urban communities across Africa. The organisation gives particular attention to vulnerable populations, including women and young people. Its development model seeks to strengthen locally led solutions while helping communities respond to the interconnected challenges of: Climate change Biodiversity loss Pollution Poverty Unemployment Food insecurity Livelihood vulnerability Gender inequality Financial exclusion Weak local economies Limited access to skills and development opportunities Green Growth Africa uses research, policy engagement, dialogue, advocacy, education, skills development and capacity building as tools for social and environmental change. Its principal thematic areas include: Environment and climate change Circular economy Agriculture and biodiversity Ecotourism and community development Socioeconomic empowerment The organisation seeks to connect environmental sustainability with local livelihoods, community institutions, gender equality, economic opportunity and social wellbeing. Why Green Growth Africa Is Recruiting Climate and development organisations increasingly operate at the intersection of community implementation, evidence generation, policy influence, partnerships and financing. Environmental projects cannot be treated as isolated technical interventions. Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution frequently overlap with poverty, unemployment, weak community institutions and limited livelihood opportunities. Green Growth Africa’s recruitment reflects the need for professionals who can: Design practical environmental and development programmes Work directly with communities Generate reliable evidence Analyse policies and legislation Mobilise donor and partnership resources Engage government institutions Strengthen local organisations Support livelihoods and enterprises Promote an inclusive circular economy Translate research into policy recommendations Document lessons and successful development models Connect local realities with national and regional policy processes Each of the three positions contributes to this wider institutional objective from a different professional perspective. Position One: Circularity and Just Transition Officer Purpose of the Position The Circularity and Just Transition Officer will support the design, coordination and implementation of Green Growth Africa’s circular economy and just-transition portfolio. The recruitment notice states that the role will pay particular attention to: Waste workers Informal-sector livelihoods Inclusive waste-management systems Resource recovery Circular economy development Fairness and social inclusion during environmental transitions The position is therefore intended to ensure that movement toward a circular and resource-efficient economy also protects workers, vulnerable communities and people earning livelihoods in informal waste-management systems. Expected Working Context Green Growth Africa’s circular economy programme promotes: Waste reduction Recycling Sustainable production Resource efficiency Community education Behavioural change Zero-waste communities Green employment Improved livelihoods Social protection for waste pickers The organisation’s zero-waste community model brings together cities, local government institutions, communities and waste-sector stakeholders to improve waste management and encourage more sustainable production and consumption. Green Growth Africa also works to equip waste pickers with alternative or complementary livelihoods and connect them with social-protection arrangements. The Circularity and Just Transition Officer is expected to operate within this broader institutional environment. Confirmed Focus Areas Based on the official recruitment summary, the position will involve supporting work connected with: Circular economy programme design Just-transition planning Waste-sector inclusion Waste-worker livelihoods Informal-sector engagement Resource-recovery systems Inclusive economic development Coordination of environmental and social priorities Implementation of Green Growth Africa’s circular economy portfolio Important Information About the Missing Terms of Reference The recruitment notice contains a shortened link for the Circularity and Just Transition Officer’s terms of reference, but that link currently returns an unavailable-page error. One of the Google Drive links supplied for this recruitment was also duplicated, meaning the complete Circularity and Just Transition Officer terms were not available for independent review. Consequently, applicants should not assume that the salary, degree requirements, experience threshold or employment conditions confirmed for the other two positions automatically apply to this role. Candidates interested in the Circularity and Just Transition Officer position should contact Green Growth Africa at info@greengrowthafrica.org and request the complete terms of reference before finalising their application or accepting an offer. Position Two: Integrated Development Officer Purpose of the Position The Integrated Development Officer will help Green Growth Africa design and implement programmes addressing environmental and socioeconomic challenges in an integrated manner. The Officer will work with rural and urban communities to identify priorities, strengthen local institutions, support livelihoods, build partnerships and develop practical solutions that improve resilience and socioeconomic wellbeing. The role is not limited to delivering predesigned projects. It also requires mobilising the financial resources, partnerships and people needed to expand Green Growth Africa’s development portfolio. Applicants can review the Integrated Development Officer terms of reference . Main Responsibilities of the Integrated Development Officer 1. Climate and Environmental Resilience The Officer will integrate climate, biodiversity and wider environmental considerations into development programmes. Responsibilities include: Supporting community-led responses to climate and environmental challenges Identifying interventions that produce environmental and socioeconomic benefits Ensuring development projects account for climate and biodiversity risks Connecting resilience-building with livelihoods and local economic development Helping communities develop practical responses to the triple planetary crises 2. Community-Led Development The Integrated Development Officer will work directly with local communities rather than designing programmes without community participation. This work will involve: Conducting participatory community assessments Identifying community-defined priorities Supporting communities in designing development initiatives Promoting local ownership of projects Strengthening community organisations Developing local leadership structures Ensuring community knowledge informs programme design Encouraging solutions that communities can sustain and scale 3. Livelihoods and Local Economic Development A major part of the position involves identifying and strengthening opportunities for livelihoods, enterprise development and income generation. The Officer will be expected to: Assess local economic opportunities Support community enterprises Work with cooperatives Assist micro, small and medium-sized enterprises Connect local organisations and businesses to markets Improve access to finance Link communities with skills and technical assistance Develop livelihood interventions that are environmentally sustainable Support enterprises capable of improving household income and resilience 4. Gender, Youth and Social Inclusion Green Growth Africa places women, young people and vulnerable groups at the centre of its work. The Integrated Development Officer will therefore: Promote meaningful participation by women and youth Support women-led enterprises Support youth-led enterprises Encourage community solutions led by underrepresented groups Ensure programme designs respond to the needs of vulnerable populations Identify participation barriers Incorporate inclusion into project planning and implementation 5. Programme Development, Funding and Partnerships The position also carries significant fundraising and partnership responsibilities. The Officer will help Green Growth Africa expand its development portfolio by: Identifying new partnership opportunities Seeking solicited and unsolicited grant funding Developing project concepts Supporting proposal preparation Exploring innovative financing arrangements Building relationships with municipalities Engaging businesses Coordinating with development organisations Establishing partnerships with communities Documenting successful models for replication Supporting organisational learning and programme growth Expected Deliverables The Integrated Development Officer may be responsible for producing or contributing to: New donor and partnership opportunities Research papers Policy briefs Community assessments Community development plans Livelihood assessments Local economic opportunity assessments Community engagement plans Capacity-building plans Project concepts Funding proposals Programme workplans Programme reports Learning products Community case studies Impact stories Documentation of replicable development models Academic Qualifications Applicants must hold at least a bachelor’s degree in one of the following areas: Development Studies Community Development Environmental Management Social Sciences Economics Another closely related discipline A master’s degree will be considered an additional advantage but is not stated as a mandatory requirement. Professional Experience Candidates must possess at least three years of relevant experience in one or more of the following fields: Community development Livelihood programmes Environmental programming Development programmes Locally led development Climate resilience Enterprise development Stakeholder engagement Programme implementation Additional Experience and Skills Strong applicants should demonstrate: Experience working directly with communities Experience working with local organisations Practical programme-implementation experience Stakeholder-engagement skills Strong written and verbal communication Facilitation skills Report-writing ability Experience in rural communities Experience in informal urban communities Knowledge of livelihoods and enterprise development Experience working with local government Experience engaging development partners Ability to mobilise partnerships and resources Commitment to inclusive and locally led development Position Three: Research and Policy Officer Purpose of the Position The Research and Policy Officer will support Green Growth Africa’s research, evidence generation, policy analysis and advocacy work. The role will focus particularly on: Air quality Zero waste Coastal livelihoods Climate change Biodiversity Pollution Circular economy Gender equality Locally led development Environmental justice Socioeconomic effects of environmental transitions The Officer will connect community experience, programme implementation, research and policy influence. Evidence generated through the role should strengthen Green Growth Africa’s programmes while helping the organisation contribute meaningfully to public policy discussions. Applicants can review the Research and Policy Officer terms of reference . Main Responsibilities of the Research and Policy Officer 1. Research and Evidence Generation The Officer will conduct applied research aligned with Green Growth Africa’s programmes and strategic priorities. Responsibilities include: Designing and conducting applied research Generating evidence from local communities Analysing programme data and implementation experience Conducting secondary research Examining climate and development challenges Investigating issues affecting rural populations Investigating issues affecting urban populations Identifying important evidence gaps Connecting research questions with organisational priorities Ensuring evidence reflects local realities The organisation expects research to be practical and grounded in community experience rather than limited to academic theory. 2. Policy Analysis and Monitoring The Research and Policy Officer will monitor policies, legislation, strategies and financing relevant to Green Growth Africa’s work. This includes: Tracking national and local policy developments Monitoring climate and environmental legislation Reviewing government strategies Following relevant financing mechanisms Analysing gaps in existing policies Evaluating implications for communities Assessing implications for local organisations Identifying opportunities for policy engagement Advising Green Growth Africa on emerging policy issues Supporting evidence-informed organisational positions 3. Knowledge Management and Organisational Learning The Officer will help Green Growth Africa capture and use knowledge emerging from its programmes.
